conceptTag: Is this café at product-market fit?
readerTitle: The line was out the door. Is this café really working?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 카페, 반려견 미용실 예약 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 카페가 시장에 맞는지는 개업 첫 주의 줄이 아니라, 처음 온 손님이 몇 달 뒤에도 다시 오는지와 그 비율이 멈추는 지점으로 판단한다.
misconception: 줄이 길고 리뷰가 좋고 매출이 오르면 제품-시장 적합성을 찾은 것이다.

sources.text: 제품-시장 적합성과 리텐션 곡선에 대한 일반적인 개념 (이 유닛의 CUS-03-03, CUS-03-06 개념 레슨)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 차트 값(주말 첫 방문 고객 100% → 2개월 차 15% → 3개월 차 8% → 4개월 차 7%, 평일 아침 첫 방문 고객 100% → 55% → 50% → 49%)이 3번·5번 카드 문장과 일치하는지 확인했습니다.
앱 사례: 첫 주 가입 3,000곳은 가상 수치입니다. 카드에 비율을 따로 적지 않아 계산 확인은 필요 없습니다.
이 레슨은 적용 레슨이므로 새 개념을 소개하지 않습니다. 사용한 개념은 CUS-03-03(리텐션)과 CUS-03-06(가짜 신호)입니다. 개념 레슨의 용어 정의와 표현이 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The line was out the door. Is this café really working?
body: Maya opened her café four months ago. On opening weekend the line reached the corner. Local food accounts posted photos. The reviews average 4.8 stars.
Sales are still growing. Her friends say she's nailed it. But Maya has noticed something: she rarely sees the same weekend faces twice.

image.label: A busy café with a long line on opening weekend
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 동네 카페 앞에 긴 줄, 사람들이 휴대폰으로 사진을 찍는 장면. 카운터 뒤 주인은 미소 짓지만 살짝 궁금한 표정. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which number should Maya check first?
body: Maya has a till that records sales and a free loyalty card that about half her customers use. She wants to know if the café truly fits its market.

options.text: Monthly sales, which are up every month so far
options.feedback: Sales matter, but rising totals can come from a stream of new, curious visitors. They hide whether anyone comes back.

options.text: How many first-time loyalty customers return in later months
options.feedback: This is **retention as the real signal**. Repeat visits show the café solved a real need, not just sparked curiosity.
Reviews are easy to collect and feel good. But early reviews often come from fans and friends, a classic **false sign of fit**.

cards.title: Two groups, two very different curves.
body: Maya sorts her loyalty customers by when they first visited. Weekend visitors mostly came once. Weekday morning customers kept coming.

groups.label: First visit on a weekday morning

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · False signs of fit
cards.title: The buzz was real. The fit wasn't.
body: The weekend crowds were mostly drawn by novelty: a new place, nice photos, a reason to try something. That kind of interest shows up fast and fades just as fast.
Long opening lines, glowing early reviews and rising sales all looked like fit. They were **false signs**: proof that people were curious, not proof that they needed the café.

image.label: Opening-day balloons deflating beside a café door
image.brief: 카페 문 옆에 'Grand opening' 풍선이 천천히 바람이 빠지는 모습. 한쪽에는 사진 찍는 손님 실루엣이 사라지고, 다른 쪽에는 출근 복장 손님 몇 명이 꾸준히 들어옴. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Look for the curve that goes flat.
body: The weekday morning curve drops at first, then holds near 50%. A curve that stops falling means a group of customers has made the café part of their routine.
That flat line is the real signal. Maya doesn't have fit with *everyone*. She has early signs of fit with commuters who want good coffee on the way to work.

options.text: Run a weekend discount to bring the crowds back
options.feedback: It may fill the room again, but discounts create another **false sign of fit**. The crowd may leave when the deal does.

options.text: Serve weekday regulars better and watch whether their curve holds
options.feedback: She builds on the one group whose **retention** has flattened. Earlier opening or faster ordering can strengthen it, and the curve tells her if it worked.

options.text: Add a brunch menu to win back weekend visitors
options.feedback: It might work, but it spends effort on the group that didn't stick. Test it small before betting on it.

cards.title: A flat curve isn't the whole answer.
body: Four months is short, and seasons change habits. Loyalty cards only show the customers who use them.
Some regulars may come back because the café is simply the closest one, not because they love it. And a flat curve only helps if that group spends enough to cover rent and staff.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app for dog groomers.
body: Your app helps dog groomers take bookings. After a launch post goes viral, 3,000 grooming shops sign up in the first week. Most log in once. Which number tells you most about fit?

options.feedback: Launch-day signups are a **false sign of fit**. They show the post spread, not that groomers rely on the app.

options.text: The share of week-one shops still taking bookings in week eight
options.feedback: This is **retention as the real signal**. If that share stops falling, some groomers have built the app into how they work.

options.text: How many feature requests users send
options.feedback: Requests show engagement and can guide you. But people who left rarely send them, so the number hides who quietly quit.

cards.softwareNote: In software, the café's loyalty card becomes a cohort table: users grouped by signup week, tracked by whether they still use the product.

cards.title: Fit shows up in who comes back, not who shows up.
body: Concepts used: **Retention as the real signal** (look for a curve that goes flat) and **False signs of fit** (buzz, reviews and early sales can mislead).
**Try it today:** pick the customers who first bought from you three months ago. Count how many bought again last month.
